title: GCMAN
summary: GCMAN is a financially motivated threat group tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as G0036, assessed in public reporting to be Russian speaking and active from roughly 2014 to 2016. Rather than deploying a large custom toolkit, the group is characterised by living off the land and by abusing legitimate remote administration software such as the Ammyy Admin tool to hold interactive access to victim networks. Reported intrusions focused on banks and payment processing environments, where operators obtained valid account credentials, moved laterally to servers that initiate money transfers, and used automated scripts to push repeated low-value transfers to mule accounts. Investigators most often recover the group's footprint from endpoint logs of remote access tool installation, unusual outbound remote desktop or support sessions, service account authentications outside business hours, and clustered payment records matching many small transfers. The overlap of legitimate administration tools with normal business activity is what makes this activity difficult to separate from routine IT operations, and it is the reason behaviour-based detection around payments and remote access tooling is emphasised in defensive guidance.

beginner.definition: GCMAN is the name security researchers give to a group of criminals who steal money from banks. They do not break into buildings or cash machines. Instead, they get into a bank's computer network and send the money out by wire transfer.
beginner.whyItMatters: When attackers reach the systems that move money, the loss is measured in millions, not in stolen files. GCMAN is also a warning about trust. They often use normal remote support software (tools that let a technician control a computer from far away), so their activity can look like everyday IT work. If nobody watches payment behaviour closely, the theft can continue for weeks before anyone notices.
howItWorks: First, the group gets a way in, usually through stolen logins or a phishing email that tricks an employee into opening an attachment.
Next, they install remote administration software so a person can control the victim computer from another country.
They gather more usernames and passwords, looking for accounts with wider access inside the bank network.
Using those accounts, they move from ordinary workstations to servers that handle payment messages and transfers.
They set up automated scripts that send many small payments to accounts controlled by helpers, called mules.
Finally, they hide the transfers among normal traffic and repeat the process until investigators spot the pattern.
beginner.example: Picture a bank at night. A cleaner with a valid badge walks in through the staff entrance. Nobody questions the badge. Once inside, the cleaner opens several locked doors, moves to the room where transfers are approved, and starts sending small payments out. The alarm never rings, because every door was opened with a real badge. GCMAN works in the same calm way. They do not force anything. They use accounts and tools that already belong in the building, which is why the bank only notices later when the records look strange.
takeaways: Attackers who want money go after payment systems, not just personal data.
Legitimate remote support tools are a favourite entry point for these groups.
Watch for many small transfers, as they are easier to hide than one large one.

objectives: Describe GCMAN at a high level and explain why it is classified as a financially motivated threat group.
Explain how abuse of legitimate remote administration software complicates detection in a corporate network.
Identify the log sources that can reveal unauthorised remote access tool installation and use.
Recognise payment fraud patterns such as repeated low-value transfers to mule accounts.
Summarise the defensive controls that reduce the value of stolen credentials in banking environments.
